transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

Whenever we’re supposed to sit and do quiet activities here, I just can’t seem to keep myself still and focused on them. My daughter actually suggested I get evaluated because it's become much more of an issue since I moved into my senior living complex.
Have you struggled with staying still and focusing throughout your life, such as during school or work, or is this a new issue that started after your recent move?

Oh, this is definitely a lifelong pattern, not a new issue. Even back in grade school, my teachers were always telling me to stay in my seat and stop blurting out answers, and my mother said I was always "on the go." It just became much more noticeable and problematic about a year and a half ago when I moved into this highly structured senior living complex.
Do you often experience constant, excessive worry about everyday things—like your health, family, or daily chores—that feels difficult to control?

No, I don't really experience constant or uncontrollable worry about those things. My main issue is more about this physical restlessness and having such a hard time staying still when I'm supposed to.
Along with the physical restlessness, do you also frequently struggle with things like making careless mistakes, losing track of your belongings, or getting easily distracted?

No, I don't really struggle with losing my things, making careless mistakes, or being easily distracted. It’s really more about my body needing to move, like feeling a jittery buzzing inside and having a hard time waiting my turn or staying seated.
How do these difficulties with staying still and waiting your turn impact your daily life, activities, or relationships with others in your community?

I've received gentle scoldings and reminders from the staff and other residents here about interrupting, pacing, and not waiting my turn. It has made me feel quite embarrassed, so I've actually started avoiding some of the group activities because it's just so hard for me to sit still and follow their routine.
During your childhood or teenage years, did you ever have a pattern of getting into serious trouble, such as frequently fighting, stealing, destroying property, or breaking major rules?

No, I never got into any serious trouble like fighting, stealing, or destroying property when I was growing up. My only issues back then were being constantly on the go, having a hard time staying in my seat, and blurting out answers in class.
Do you find it difficult to sustain your attention on tasks like reading, or do you often feel like your mind is wandering when someone is speaking directly to you?

No, I don't really have trouble with reading or my mind wandering when someone is speaking directly to me. My main challenge is more about the physical restlessness and that constant urge to keep moving, rather than losing my focus in those ways.
When you were growing up, did you often lose your temper, argue with adults, or actively defy rules and requests?

No, I don't recall having those specific issues like losing my temper or defying rules when I was growing up. I just remember having a lot of energy, being unable to sit still, and constantly blurting things out in class.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a clear, lifelong pattern of prominent hyperactive and impulsive symptoms, including physical restlessness, difficulty staying seated, pacing, interrupting, and difficulty waiting her turn, with onset dating back to grade school. These symptoms cause functional impairment in her current social environment (senior living complex) and meet the criteria for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Presentation (ICD-10-CM: F90.1). She does not meet the criteria for inattention, conduct disorder, or anxiety disorders.
